case_study_insert.main_stem: Treetop Canopy Lodges (TCL) is a private limited company in the leisure and tourism sector, operating forest eco-pods and canopy walkways in a northern rainforest reserve. Founded in 2015 by Nathan Oyelaran, it employs a workforce of 90 and uses a flat structure with laissez-faire leadership. TCL plans to invest $750,000 in twelve new treehouse pods with automated eco-sensors, financed by a $400,000 ten-year bank loan and a $350,000 share issue. It has fixed costs of $360,000 a year, a variable cost of $40 a unit and a selling price of $140, and currently produces 15,000 units a year. TCL faces rising labour turnover among its guides and a worsening guest complaint rate about pod maintenance.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Operations and Quality Report — Q4 2026: TCL sold 15,000 guest-nights (units) last year, up from 13,200 a year ago. Pod maintenance rework affected 5.8% of stays, down from 8.1% previously. Guest complaints fell from 36 to 19 per month, and average check-in time is 3.1 minutes. A survey of 420 guests found that 71% would pay a $25 premium for canopy-view pods and 58% prefer to book through the mobile app. Team working is used across the guide and maintenance teams. On-the-job training covers routine checks, while off-the-job training at the regional centre costs $620 per employee; 14 of the 90 staff need recertification on the new monitoring systems.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Treetop Canopy Lodges as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.25% to 5.0%, raising the cost of variable-rate borrowing. (2) The national minimum wage rises by 5.8% from $14.00 to $14.81 per hour from May 2026, increasing wage bills for leisure operators. (3) Fuel and timber input costs have risen 9.4% year-on-year, while domestic tourism spending grew 5.6% over the same period.

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages for TCL of using a share issue rather than the bank loan to help fund the $750,000 treehouse-pod expansion.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: A share issue brings in $350,000 of equity that carries no interest and no fixed repayment dates, unlike the $400,000 ten-year bank loan. With $360,000 of annual fixed costs already committed, TCL avoids the 0.75% rise in borrowing cost and preserves cash to absorb the 9.4% increase in fuel and timber inputs, protecting the $100 contribution per unit ($140 − $40) on its 15,000 guest-nights.

Point 2: The new shareholders share the risk of the twelve pods with automated eco-sensors, so Nathan Oyelaran's business is not solely exposed if the 5.8% minimum wage rise pushes costs up or the worsening guest complaints delay bookings. Equity also strengthens the statement of financial position shown in appendix 2, giving TCL more headroom than piling another loan onto existing debt before the $750,000 programme is complete.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to TCL's financing decision.

questions.question_text: Consider national eco-travel magazine advertising, local radio sponsorship, or partnerships with specialist outdoor tourism websites. Which should TCL choose to promote its new canopy-view pods? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
National eco-travel magazine advertising: A full-page campaign in national magazines would build prestige for TCL's forest reserve and reach educated travellers who might pay the $25 premium for canopy-view pods. The downside is high production and media cost against $360,000 of fixed costs, long lead times, and waste: most readers will never visit a northern rainforest reserve, and a static photograph cannot show the automated eco-sensors.

Local radio sponsorship: Local radio is inexpensive and reaches listeners near the reserve, which suits last-minute stays, but TCL's 15,000 guest-nights are drawn from a much wider catchment than one local area. A short audio message also cannot demonstrate the pods or capture the 58% of surveyed guests who prefer to book through the app, so bookings would be limited.

Partnerships with specialist outdoor tourism websites: Listing the pods on sites used by hikers and eco-travellers targets exactly the guests described in appendix 1 — the 71% of 420 surveyed guests who would pay a $25 premium — and links straight to online booking. Costs are largely performance-based, results are measurable, and the site can display the canopy views and eco-sensor features. Reach is narrower than a national magazine, but the audience is far better qualified.

Recommendation: TCL should choose partnerships with specialist outdoor tourism websites. They reach the precise segment willing to pay the premium, support the app booking channel and cost less than print. National magazine advertising is rejected as costly and geographically wasteful, and local radio is rejected as too narrow to sustain 15,000 guest-nights; TCL can add small in-resort signage as a support.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited outline of the promotional options with minimal application to TCL.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of the advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of TCL with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of TCL with a well-justified recommendation explaining why magazine advertising and local radio are rejected.

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits for TCL of using team working to improve motivation among its guides and pod-maintenance staff.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Team working suits TCL's flat structure and gives its 90 employees shared responsibility for the canopy walkways and pod maintenance, satisfying social needs and raising job satisfaction. Guides and maintenance staff who plan rotas together are more likely to attend reliably, directly tackling the rising labour turnover and the worsening guest complaint rate about pod upkeep.

Point 2: Small teams can swap practical knowledge about the automated eco-sensors, so faults are spotted earlier and the 5.8% pod maintenance rework rate can fall further from its 8.1% level. Stronger team commitment also reduces the need to replace leavers, saving part of the $620 per employee course cost for the 14 of the 90 staff needing recertification while protecting the 15,000 guest-nights sold each year.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to TCL's turnover, rework and output.

questions.question_text: TCL must upskill 14 of its 90 staff on the new automated eco-sensors. Consider on-the-job training or off-the-job training at the regional centre. Which should TCL choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job training: Senior guides can coach the 14 staff beside the actual pods and canopy walkways, so the training is specific to TCL's own monitoring systems, costs no course fees and keeps everyone available for the 15,000 guest-nights. It also lets teams immediately apply fixes that push the 5.8% rework rate down. The drawback is that coaching guides have less time for their own duties, and without a formal certificate the skills may be hard to verify if guests question safety procedures.

Off-the-job training: The regional centre course at $620 per employee, $8,680 in total for 14 people, offers structured teaching and a recognised certificate, which is modest next to the $750,000 pod programme. It takes staff away from the reserve during busy periods, however, and generic content may not match TCL's exact eco-sensors, so site coaching would still be required afterwards.

Decision: TCL should choose on-the-job training led by experienced guides, followed later by short certified modules for lead technicians. This is cheaper, specific to the pods and avoids losing capacity while labour turnover is a concern. Full off-the-job training is rejected because removing 14 of 90 staff would disrupt the guest-complaint improvement and the $620 fee can be spent later on the formal recertification the new systems need.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with limited application to TCL.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of the training methods in the context of TCL.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both training methods in the context of TCL with a well-justified decision covering cost, disruption and equipment relevance.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how TCL's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $360,000 ÷ ($140 − $40) = $360,000 ÷ $100 = 3,600 units. Answer: break-even output is 3,600 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $140 − $40 = $100. Answer: contribution per unit is $100.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways TCL's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Break-even and margin of safety: 15,000 guest-nights against a 3,600-unit break-even leaves 11,400 units of buffer, showing how far bookings can fall before the pods lose money.
2. Pricing: at $140 a unit the $100 contribution covers the $360,000 fixed costs after 3,600 units, so any discount to tourism websites must keep contribution positive.
3. Financing: the $100 contribution indicates the extra guest-nights needed to service the $400,000 bank loan and justify the $750,000 pod programme.
4. Cost benchmarking: average total cost is $64 ($360,000 ÷ 15,000 + $40), and labour productivity is 15,000 ÷ 90 = about 167 units per employee, a baseline for judging the 5.8% rework and the 36-to-19 complaint fall.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 3,600 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $100 | (iii) Four contextual uses: margin of safety of 11,400 units against 15,000 sold; pricing discipline at $140 with $100 contribution; covering the $400,000 loan and $750,000 expansion; and benchmarking at $64 a unit with labour productivity of about 167 units per employee to tackle the 5.8% rework.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method, 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate TCL's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has TCL's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.12 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.16 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.82 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 0.85 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $45,000 inventories + $85,000 trade receivables + $38,000 cash = $168,000; against $150,000 of short-term obligations this gives 1.12, and excluding inventories $123,000 ÷ $150,000 = 0.82. In 2025 current assets = $52,000 + $96,000 + $44,000 = $192,000 against $165,000 owed, giving 1.16; without stock, $140,000 ÷ $165,000 = 0.85.

Evaluation: Liquidity improved only slightly. The broad measure moved from 1.12 to 1.16 because current assets rose by $24,000 while current liabilities rose by $15,000, helped by cash climbing from $38,000 to $44,000. The stricter measure, which removes inventories, rose from 0.82 to 0.85 but remains below 1, so TCL still cannot cover near-term debts without relying on stock — a concern while it services a $400,000 loan and funds the $750,000 pod programme. Trade receivables also grew from $85,000 to $96,000, tying up cash; if guests and tour operators pay late, these thin margins could disappear.

Conclusion: TCL's financial position has improved, but only marginally. Both measures are higher and the stricter measure is less stock-dependent, yet with cover still under 1 on that measure the improvement is modest, so managers should tighten credit control before committing further to the expansion.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the current ratio and acid test ratio for both 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years combined with detailed evaluation of inventories, receivables and liabilities movements and a justified conclusion on whether TCL's financial position improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for TCL of offering canopy-view pods at a $25 premium.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: The $25 premium is supported by appendix 1, where 71% of 420 surveyed guests would pay more for canopy-view pods and 58% already book through the app. It lifts revenue above the $140 base price and defends the $100 contribution per unit as fuel and timber input costs rise 9.4% and the 5.8% wage increase takes effect, helping TCL justify the $750,000 investment in twelve new pods.

Disadvantage: Building and maintaining canopy-view pods with automated eco-sensors is likely to raise the $40 variable cost per unit and add to the $360,000 fixed costs, so margins could be squeezed if fewer than the surveyed 71% actually pay the premium. The 5.8% pod maintenance rework rate could also worsen if the new structures need specialist attention, deepening the guest complaints about pod upkeep just as the new pods open.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to TCL's research data, costs and expansion.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the rise in the base interest rate to 5.0%, the 5.8% minimum wage increase and the 9.4% rise in input costs will affect TCL. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Base interest rate rise from 4.25% to 5.0%: If TCL's $400,000 ten-year bank loan is variable-rate, the 0.75-point rise adds 0.75% × $400,000 = $3,000 a year (0.0075 × $400,000). That is modest against $360,000 of fixed costs, and if the loan is fixed-rate there is no extra charge. Higher rates may still reduce guests' discretionary spending on forest breaks, but TCL can cap this exposure by fixing the rate.

Minimum wage rise of 5.8% from $14.00 to $14.81 per hour: With a workforce of 90 this raises the wage bill and cannot be avoided. The insert does not state hours worked or individual pay, so an annual total cannot be invented. The defensible test is productivity: 15,000 units ÷ 90 staff = about 167 units per employee, so the rise is affordable only if productivity holds or guest-nights grow; otherwise unit labour cost rises and the $100 contribution falls.

Input-cost inflation of 9.4%: The insert never decomposes the $40 variable cost, so only a bound can be shown: if all $40 were exposed, 9.4% × $40 = $3.76 a unit, which at 15,000 guest-nights is $56,400 a year. A smaller exposed share would cost proportionally less. TCL can recover part through the $25 canopy-view premium that 71% of 420 surveyed guests said they would pay.

Conclusion: The 9.4% input-cost inflation has the greatest impact. It hits every one of the 15,000 guest-nights and directly erodes the $100 contribution that underpins the $750,000 pod programme, while the interest effect is only $3,000 and the wage effect depends on unknown hours. TCL should seek fixed-price supply deals and promote the $25 premium.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to TCL.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on TCL's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of TCL with a well-justified judgement that input-cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the others are smaller.
